As requested, we created TAK1 RR-D/E-S variants and tested the dephosphorylation efficiency for CN . The data show that both variants are more efficiently dephosphorylated by CN than wt-TAK1.
These data have been added to the revised manuscript (Figure 4g). We thank the reviewer for this suggestion, which further strengthens the results of our work.
4. The variant 436RRVS439 should be characterized in the functional dephosphorylation assay. This concerns all the other variants where ITC affinities and dehosphorylation potential should be determined.
As requested, we have performed dephosphorylation assays of the TAK1 RR-V-S variant vs CN , which showed the expected outcome.
These data have been added to the revised manuscript (Figure 4g). We thank the reviewer for this suggestion, which further strengthens the results of our work.
5. Chapter “Arginine in the i-1 position is a general mechanism for enhanced CN substrate dephosphorylation” – contrary to the title, the data presented in this chapter does not show the generality of the arginine mechanism. A single example is provided in support of the proposed mechanism, but single example does not allow to conclude on generality. Omic analysis of substrates could possibly allow to conclude on generality of the proposed mechanism, but even than authors should reconcile how substrates like 96RRVS99 get dephosphorylated when they show that -2 and -3 sites are less relevant (or irrelevant) for recognition.
We agree with the reviewer that a single example is not enough to test (or claim) generality. It is for this reason that we expanded from TAK1 to RII. RII is a canonical CN substrate (likely the substrate used most often to confirm CN activity). We tested if substituting the RII Vi-1 residue to an Ri-1 residue would enhance dephosphorylation efficiency. It did, and this is what we reported in the submitted manuscript (Figure 3). Next, as suggested by the reviewer, we also performed Omic analysis, first leveraging an in vitro peptide analysis/assay and second a cellular analysis using HEK293T and now also N2A cells (please see below).
The reviewer is concerned (asking) why wt RII, which has a RRVS dephosphorylation sequence, is still dephosphorylated by CN. Clearly, RRVS sequences are still viable CN dephosphorylation sites, they are just not as effectively/efficiently dephosphorylated as RRRS sites (even in the title, we highlight that is an enhancement and not an on/off switch). A key aspect of CN dephosphorylation is that CN substrates must first be recruited to CN via SLiM motifs (PxIxIT and/or LxVP). It is only after recruitment that active site recognition sequences can enhance dephosphorylation. For RII:CN, RII is recruited to CN via its LxVP motif leading to wt-RII dephosphorylation (shown in Figure 3). However, while wt-RII is clearly dephosphorylated by CN, this dephosphorylation is enhanced when the Vi-1 is mutated to Ri-1.
Thus, in a scenario where a CN substrate with a single LxVP motif yet multiple phosphorylated residues (the most studied example is the NFATs), our data shows that the RRRS phosphosites, versus RRVS phosphosites, will be more rapidly dephosphorylated. Using similar experiments, we previously discovered that S/TxxP motifs are also preferentially dephosphorylated by CN (see Nature Communication. 2019 Aug 2;10(1):3489).
Regarding the reduced importance of the i-2/i-3 sites: the reviewer is correct these sites are not important for enhanced substrate recruitment to CN (shown by additional ITC and activity assays, Figures 4 and S4). However, these arginine residues do have an essential biological role as they are critical for the preceding event: phosphorylation. That is, PKA is an Arg-directed kinase, with a consensus sequence of R-R-x-S/T; i.e., the i-2/i-3 arginines ensure these TAK1/RII sequences are phosphorylated by PKA.
We hope this explanation and data clarify the issues at hand – we have added a sentence to the discussion to make this clearer. Thank you for pointing out that additional information will be helpful for the general reader.
6. “crystal structure of a substrate trapped CN complex” – the manuscript text states “tethered to the PxIxIT site using the A238L viral inhibitor peptide”, Figure 2a and the further manuscript text discuss binding at LxVP site. Please, clarify. Also, please clarify what “A238L viral inhibitor peptide” is, and detail in the main text on the design of the thiphosphorylated TAK1 and CN constructs that were used for crystallization.
We thank the reviewer for highlighting that additional information will be helpful for clarity. First, we want to point out that immediately after the statement “tethered to the PxIxIT site using the A238L viral inhibitor peptide” is a reference to Supplementary Figs. 3a,b, which provide additional information. In addition, reference 21 refers to our manuscript that describes the structure of CN in complex with the potent (K = 4 nM) protein regulator A238L, which is a protein from the African swine fever virus.
During the last 20 years, it has become apparent that CN crystallizes much more readily when one or both of its SLiM sites is/are occupied (i.e. bound to a regulator/substrate). By design, substrates typically engage weakly at enzyme active sites (otherwise they would be inhibitors). Thus, to ‘trap’ substrates at active sites, different strategies are used. One of the most common is to artificially tether the substrate, i.e. via their C/N-terminus, to the enzyme to increase their ‘local concentration’. We did not want to use an artificial tethering approach but rather leveraged a ‘biologically existing tether’: a modified A238L peptide which contains the TAK1 sequence starting from the LxVP site (as described in detail in the figure caption of Supplementary Figure 3 as well as in the methods section – see A238L-TAK1 chimera in cloning [where we also provide its full aa sequence] and expression and purification). This tethering has the key advantage that we know how A238L binds to CN and thus fitting the new electron density due to the RRRS motif is straightforward and is much less likely to be misinterpreted. We hope this explanation clarifies the rational as well as highlights all the details provided in the methods and figure legends of the manuscript.
7. RII dephosphorylation – the difference in dephosphorylation rate for WT enzyme and E237K and 282K mutants is significant already for WT substrate. How would the authors explain this effect? In addition, it would be interesting to test if similar is true when TAK1 RRVS is used.
The reviewer is correct pointing out that there is a dephosphorylation rate difference for RII between CN and CN and CN . This was not surprising for us as the different conformation of TAK1 in complex with CN in the two molecules in the unit cell already highlighted that the interaction is dynamic (fuzzy; we also highlight this explicitly in the manuscript). Thus, the substrate can ‘move’ and adapt to the optimal position for dephosphorylation, as observed in the presented data. While we were able to visualize a subset of positions that TAK1 can adopt when bound to CN – there are likely additional conformations that are not stable enough (populated enough) to be seen in the crystal structure. Furthermore, there are likely even more degrees of freedom for the interaction in the variants that also show reduced binding to TAK1. Finally, as already shown in response to comment 4, we have now also performed a dephosphorylation assay for the TAK1 RR-V-S variant vs CN . These data have been added to the revised manuscript (Figure 4).
8. “we determined the crystal structure of CNE282K“ – to my understanding this is not a structure of CNE282K alone, but in complex with NHE1. If so, this should be indicated in the sentence “we determined the crystal structure of CNE282K in complex with HNE1”. The text should also address the question why catalytically dead CN variant was necessary to crystalize with TAK1 while it was possible to crystallize HNE1 with active (I assume) CN?
The reviewer is correct that the crystal structure of CN was determined in complex with NHE1. As highlighted in our response to point 6 – CN crystallizes more readily when its SLiM binding pockets are populated. We crystallized CN bound to NHE1 not only to facilitate its crystallization but to also confirm that its SLiM binding pockets are not negatively impacted by the E282K mutation. The sentence in the manuscript highlighted by the reviewer reads as follows: “we determined the crystal structure of CN (Fig. 4b; bound to NHE1, a substrate that binds CN using a PxIxIT and LxVP motif).” This directly reports that we determined the structure of CN in complex with NHE1 – we try to be as transparent as possible with all of our work. All experimental details, including the full sequences, are also provided in the methods section.
The reviewer wants to know why we had to use a catalytically inactive variant of CN to get the structure of TAK1 – a substrate – bound to CN, while it was not necessary for NHE1. For TAK1 we trapped the substrate bound to the CN active site using a (thio)phosphorylated substrate; if we had formed the complex with active CN, the substrate would have been dephosphorylated, and we would not have been able to observe the interactions made at the CN active site between a phosphorylated substrate and CN. Indeed, to prevent dephosphorylation – we used multiple ‘tricks’, including using the inactive CN variant and thiophosphorylating the substrate (even thiophosphorylated substrates are slowly dephosphorylated).
While NHE1 is a CN substrate, the construct we used for crystallization lacks the dephosphorylation residues (these are 50+aa beyond the CN SLiM interaction motifs) and only includes the SLiM interaction motifs. Here, NHE1 was solely used to stabilize CN for crystallization and thus there was no need to use a catalytically inactive variant of CN.
9. Is the (i-1) arginine containing structure exceptional or had there been other structures earlier (if so should be discussed in the introduction)
To the best of our knowledge the (i-1) arginine containing structure is exceptional. To the best of our knowledge, this is also the first CN structure with any substrate bound to the active site. We have refrained from using ‘first’ throughout the manuscript, as this is generally not accepted per most journals’ policies.
10. My major comment pertains to the phosphoproteome study. The study on phosphopeptides isolated form HeLa cells clearly shows a shift in substrate preference in E282K variant of CN. The particular experiment provides a clear indication of the shift, but only allows to conclude on the shift in a completely nonphysiologically model. The substrates, though diverse, are short peptides and not full proteins – therefore most of the complexity of substrate recognition is lost. Secondly, HeLa cell proteome is largely irrelevant for CN, especially in the context of neurodevelopmental pathologies related to E282K and treatment with pan-PPP inhibitor likely induces significant non-physiological phosphorylation. Further, digestion with Lys-C removes all potential Lys sites (it would also be interesting to test if R(i-1) can be substituted with K using the peptide substrates from the initial part of the study (TAK1); it should be explicitly stated on the panel d in figure 5 that the assay is not capable of detecting lysine containing substrates).
To evaluate the substrate preference at more physiological conditions, authors overexpress the CN in 293T cells (is it in CN negative background?). This allows to assess intact proteomes (rather than over-phosphorylated peptide mixture), but the choice of cell line is irrelevant to CN and PPP3CA related DEE.
The reviewer is correct with her/his statements and summarizes effectively our intended design. We used HeLa cells to generate a phosphorylated library of peptides to assay CN vs CN active site dephosphorylation preferences. Our use of short peptides minimizes the chance that any CN-specific SLiMs are present in the peptides – this is by design, as the presence of SLiMs would reduce the significance of the observed active site motifs and thus would be counterproductive. We selected HeLa cells because they are easy to work with, allowing the ‘general’ phosphopeptide library to be readily generated. In short, the goal of this study was to use the HeLa-generated phosphorylated library of peptides to determine if/how the active site substrate preference shifts because of the E282K mutation (i.e., CN to CN ).
The author is also correct that next we tested dephosphorylation changes in HEK293T cells. While we agree that HEK293Ts are not perfect cell lines, ≥90% of all reported MS data is from HEK293T experiments, enabling us to compare our data with existing, comprehensive databases.
But we also agree with the reviewer that one should always try to provide data from cell lines relevant to the system under investigation. Thus, in response to the reviewer, we now also performed the MS experiments using N2A cells. N2A cells are a commonly used mouse neuronal cell line. The N2A results show a similar trend as the HeLa phosphorylated peptide library and the HEK293T MS data. All these data, including those from HEK293T and N2A cells, are included in this revised manuscript (Figure 6 and Supplemental Figures).
Lastly, the reviewer comments that we should also test if Lys can substitute for Arg in the -1 position. To answer this question, we generated a TAK1 RR-K-S variant and measured its dephosphorylation. As expected, dephosphorylation is similar to wt-TAK1 (RR-R-S) and further confirms our results (Figure 4).
These data have been added to the revised manuscript. We thank the reviewer for these suggestions, which further strengthened the conclusions of our work.
It would be beneficial if the authors could confirm their findings analyzing the effect of CN mutation on intact proteome in a cell line relevant to the major pathology, for example by comparative analysis of heterozygous neuronal cell line with E282 mutation compared to homozygous wt cell line, or similar, physiologically relevant setup which could provide clues as to the major imbalances in phosphorylation leading to the pathogenesis of the disease. Authors are strongly encourage to try to address this comment, however it may be difficult experimentally and thus should not preclude publication of this interesting manuscript.
We fully agree with the reviewer and indeed we are working on such experiments. CN iPSC E282K cells are currently being created by the Simmons foundation, and we are also creating a heterozygous CN mouse. Clearly, we plan to use these tools in additional experiments in the future (2026-2030), including the reviewer’s requested experiments. These tools will be made fully available to the research community for further testing in future experiments. However, as the reviewer highlights, these experiments are difficult, very time-consuming and, in our case, ongoing. We very much appreciate that the reviewer highlights that these efforts should ‘not preclude publication of this interesting manuscript’.
What we have been able to do, and as discussed above, is perform the MS experiments using a mouse neuronal cell line (N2A); these results have been added to the revised manuscript.
As it is, the data does not substantiate the conclusion that “These data (…), highlights how a single point variant, CNE282K, globally alters the CN substrate recruitment and dephosphorylation.” as the recruitment and dephosphorylation of full length substrates in a cellular context relevant to PPP3CA related DEE may be significantly different.
We are not certain that we fully understand these concerns of the reviewer and, in particular, why the reviewer would think that the recruitment of full-length substrates might be different in cells. Data from many groups (including ours) have shown that SLiM-based substrate recruitment is both necessary and sufficient for the cellular fidelity observed in cells. This has been shown not only for CN, but also for a plethora of other signaling enzymes, including kinases and phosphatases. If the reviewer refers to the fact that SLiM residues can be modified by post-translational modification (PTM) themselves, and thus modify signaling outcomes, that is certainly correct and another layer of the complex signaling network. However, at this point, a PTM that modifies a CN SLiM has not been reported.
Taken together, our data highlights that there is a different active site preference for substrate dephosphorylation between CN and CN . If recruitment of a CN substrate via CN SLiMs to CN is identical (as we show in our crystal structures), dephosphorylation of Ri-1 containing substrates will be slower in CN than for wt-CN; these differences in dephosphorylation rates/preferences can/do alter CN signaling networks.
If the reviewer highlights that, at this point, we have not identified all relevant substrates that are changed – that is 100% correct. This is indeed a very important and complex task that we will pursue in the next (likely 10) years. What makes this even harder is the fact that we simply do not have a very good understanding of the CN interactome/proteome (for that matter this is true for all ser/thr protein phosphatases). As already highlighted, we are producing the CN mouse to test for signaling differences – however, because of this study, we will initially focus on Ri-1 substrates. We hope that these future studies will indeed identify substrates that have a changed phosphorylation profile in CN vs wt-CN that might lead to new treatments for one or more secondary conditions (pain/epilepsy/others) of this disease. Clearly this will take years to come to full fruition.
Overall, we present work that spans molecular biology to biochemistry to structural biology to cellular MS work. This comprehensive picture allows us, and many others, to leverage these data and provide the necessary next steps for concrete strategies and hypotheses for helping PPP3CA DEE91 patients. This is an open problem and an opportunity to be tackled in the next 5-10 years.
11. As it is now, the authors should tone down the conclusion stated in the title regarding global shift of substrate dephosphorylation profile. They should also tone down the claims that activity of the mutant have been studied in cells – it indeed was, but not in cells relevant to the pathology of interest.
We thank the reviewer for her/his input. Indeed, our MS studies have been done in HEK293T and now also neuronal N2A cells; thus, we have studied the activity of the CN variant in a biologically relevant cell line. Many published MS studies have been performed in HEK293T cells. N2A is a mouse neuronal cell line, and we have now repeated the MS analysis and report on the outcome.
We agree with the reviewer that the next logical step will be a (or multiple) mouse model(s) to study the effects of this CN variant further. While this is beyond our current scope, it clearly does not change the impact of the conclusions of our existing, comprehensive data. Indeed, I would argue that all future studies will dramatically gain from these detailed molecular biochemical and MS analyses, which are missing from many studies that start with mouse models. We have edited the manuscript to ensure the tone is appropriate for the results.
Minor comments;
1. Abstract – if calcineurin is abbreviated CN in the text, this abbreviation should be the first one in the list of abbreviations given in the first sentence “(PP3CA; CN, Protein Phosphatase 2B [PP2B], PP3”).
Thank you – changed as requested.
2. “To quantify the contribution of the CN residues for TAK1 recruitment and dephosphorylation, we mutated these residues and measured their ability to dephosphorylate TAK1 pSer439”. First part of the sentence – which residues?; CN has many residues and it is unclear what is meant here. Second part of the sentence – residues with “ability to dephosphorylate TAK1” implies active site (catalytic) residues. It is unlikely that this was meant in the sentence. The entire sentence should be corrected referring to specific residues and their functions.
Thank you – we have added new data and changed this sentence/paragraph to clearly highlight which residue is referred both on TAK1 and CN.
3. “The regulatory subunit B (CNB) binds four Ca2+ ions, making CN responsive to calcium signaling.” – A sentence above mentions that CNA has a calmodulin binding site which is likely to already “make CN responsive to calcium”. The role of calmodulin binding site mediated regulation and CNB regulation should be described in few sentences.
Much of this basic knowledge about CN has been described in reviews, which are cited throughout the manuscript. However, some of the details regarding CN activation by Ca2+ have not yet been explored at molecular detail. In particular, the role of Calmodulin binding to CN and the mechanism of its subsequent activation has been not well studied nor well-defined. It is assumed that Calmodulin binding releases the autoinhibitory domain (AID); however, to the best of our knowledge, how this is achieved has not been experimentally shown. Ca2+-binding to CNB ensures that LxVP SLiMs can bind to CN. We would prefer to leave the introduction as is and focus on the new insights gained in the manuscript (multiple foundational manuscripts and reviews are referenced for further information in the introduction). But the reviewer is correct we should indeed revisit Ca2+-activation of CN and develop a detailed model in vitro.
4. It is mentioned that E282K is the most common mutation. It would be useful to map other known mutations resulting in similar clinical outcomes at the structure of CN and speculate as to their influence on the phosphoproteome. For example, is E237K a clinically relevant variant – one would expect so given the data shown in Figure 3b.
If excessive number of mutations is known, such discussion could be presented in detail in the supporting information.
There are several published manuscripts that report on clinical CN variants – these are carefully cited in the manuscript. However, beyond these published reports, we are in contact with the group of families that founded the PPP3CA Hope Foundation, which aims to collect clinical data from families around the world. This has been (partially) successful, but that data has not been made public. As said, we are working with them and are urging them to make the data available – even if only posted on their webpage. Nevertheless, the literature described variant data is very accurate and cited throughout our manuscript.
To the best of our knowledge, E237K is not a clinical variant; alternatively, if it is a clinical variant, it has not yet been identified or reported.
5. The functional sites within CN discussed in the text should all be depicted in figure 1a (ex. SLiM binding site, calmodulin binding region, auto inhibitory domain, calcium binding sites, etc.), either in 2D or 3D representation.
The reviewer is correct to point this out – but indeed this is much harder to achieve than a linear SLiM sequence on an IDP. Binding surfaces are 3-dimensional in a folded protein (e.g. the LxVP site includes residues from CNA and CNB etc.). Thus, this is hard to show in the depiction in Figure 1a. But the PxIxIT and LxVP sites are highlighted on the 3D structure of CN both in Figure 4 and in Supplemental Figures.
6. The introduction states “Mutating either of these SLiMs abolishes their ability to be dephosphorylated by CN…”. But the tested substrate (TAK1 fragment) contains only the LxVP SLiM. This apparent discrepancy should be clarified (and Figure 1a updated accordingly if necessary)
The introduction provides a general concept for CN. Most regulators and substrates indeed have both SLiM sequences and the statement is correct. The reviewer is correct that TAK1 only has a LxVP site. We hope this clarifies the statement.
7. The authors mention several times that their results “lead to the development of novel routes for treating PPP3CA-related DEE”. The results are interesting and explain the molecular pathology in PPP3CA-related DEE, but I do not see how this knowledge might lead to a treatment. With the described functional mechanism it is difficult to imagine small molecular weight compounds restoring the specivicity of CN vairant while genetic correction does not require the knowledge gained through this study. Authors are kindly requested to elaborate on their view or remove the statements pertaining to influence of their results on treatment development.
The reviewer is correct that it is unlikely that a small molecular weight compound will be effective in treating all the complications associated with a heterozygous CN . However, it is important to know that treatments can also mean simply treating one or more of the underlying associated complications (epilepsy, pain, others). Our work sets the much-needed stage for developing such strategies. We will perform additional MS experiments using iPSC patient derived cells (hopefully by mid-2026) – such as the ones now reported for N2A cells to specifically start to understand proteins that are the target of CN and differentially regulated in CN . Over the next years we will then test these findings/substrate changes in vitro and in cells. Furthermore, and as already highlighted, we are creating the heterozygous CN mouse (hopefully available also in mid-2026 for experiments). Based on our data we will focus on CN substrates with R-1 signatures (and expanded signatures that are summarized in Fig. 5 and 6). As done by many others working on rare diseases, we hope to identify specific signaling pathways that are influenced by the CN variants, which may be regulated by enzymes that already have FDA approved drugs, and their use in PPP3CA-related DEE91 patients might be possible.
Clearly this approach is not unique to CN but is also actively being used for a variety of rare diseases that arise due to spontaneous mutations in signaling enzymes. The advantage for the CN community is that we defined how this mutation changes CN function and signaling, which our community can now leverage in future analyses.
8. Figure 1a; TAK1; it is unclear what CN SLiM refers to (ie. which part of the protein)
We thank the reviewer for this question: Indeed, CN SLiM does not refer to any part of the protein, but rather CN SLiM indicates the two SLiMs highlighted next to it – the LxVP and RRRS site in TAK1. Based on the reviewers’ feedback, we can see that this might be easily misunderstood and deleted CN SLiM from the figure to improve clarity – thank you.
9. “CN counteracts the activities of many basophilic kinases, including PKA, and its sequence contains a putative LxVP motif (422LDVP425) near the PKA phosphorylation site,2” – “its sequence” points at CN in this sentence while it refers to TAK1. Please, rephrase.
Thank you – we changed the sentence to:
The amino acid sequence of TAK1 contains a putative LxVP motif (422LDVP425) near the PKA phosphorylation site,22 therefore we tested if TAK1 binds CN using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC).
10. “TAK1 bound CN with an atypically strong affinity compared to other LxVPpeptide:CN interactions (TAK1 KD, 860 ± 23 nM; Fig. 1b; other LxVP KD’s, ~1800-500000 nM; Table S1),21,23,33” – please, clarify the nomenclature – LxVPpeptide seems to signify a peptide consisting only of LxVP. Additionally, summarize the data on LxVP KD’s in a supporting figure giving exactly the constructs and affinity determination methods used to determine the affinity and construct alignment if significant differences between the constructs are present.
Thank you: to clarify the issue, we deleted the word other and replaced it with reported. The sentence now reads:
TAK1 bound CN with an atypically strong affinity compared to reported LxVPpeptide:CN interactions (TAK1 KD, 860 ± 23 nM; Fig. 1b; other LxVP KD’s, ~1800-500000 nM; Table S1),21,23,33 suggesting that residues outside the LxVP motif also contribute to binding.
The highlighted references provide ITC or SPR measurements for LxVP SLiMs in proteins and peptides. In particular, reference 33 reports on several LxVP :CN interactions measured by SPR and highlights the range of affinities measured. There, we show that the binding strength of intrinsically disordered proteins with LxVP motifs is sequence independent; rather, it depends on the k rate, i.e. it depends on the ensemble of conformations of the IDP and how that ensemble ‘presents’ the LxVP motif to CN for binding (accessibility and conformation). Since paper 33 provides such comprehensive data, we refer to this primary literature.
11. Figure 2f – please, indicate which residues constitute the -3, -2 sites and which build the -1 site.
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. A correlation between the TAK1 sequence and the Arg residues as well as how Arg sites correspond to the CN residues are established in Figure 2d/e just adjacent to Figure 2f. In particular, we used the same color code between Figure 2e and Figure 2f to ensure this can be readily understood. We hope these correlations clarify the issue. Thank you.
12. Use consistent labeling of residues (ie. Glu282 or E282) through the manuscript
Thank you – done. We have decided to keep Glu where we describe the structure and the molecular interaction but use E when the variant is described. This is meant to facilitate readability.
13. Please, use a common nomenclature throughout the manuscript. Why is CND90A:tpTAK1-tpS439 not simply called CND90A:tpTAK1 in Figure 2 legend? Especially that it has a different description in the figure title and panel legends.
Thank you – updated.
14. Figure 2, panel d – label E282 and other important residues at the figure
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion, but as highlighted in our response to point 11, these residues are all labeled in Figure 2e, which is directly next to Figure 2d. Indeed, the design of the figure was as follows: In Figure 2d we focus on the identification of all TAK1 residues, in Figure 2e we correlate these with CN residues and finally in Figure 2f show the effect of changes in the CN pockets that are displayed in Figure 2e.
We would feel that adding too much information into a single figure make the figures even harder to follow and would appreciate the possibility of keeping all three figures. Thank you.
15. Figure 2e – please suggest a more comprehensive depiction of ionic interactions. An ionic interaction is not an interaction of a particular atom in a COO- moiety as currently suggested by the figure. (ex. Asp285-Arg(-2) or Glu237-Arg (-1)).
We have changed the figure as requested and now highlight only a small number of interactions that are shorter than 4 Å and thus clearly contribute to the interaction. Thank you.
16. Figure 4b legend – make clear that both the structure of wt and mutant were determined in complex with HNE1. As currently is, it is not clear if CN(E282K) apo is not compared to WT with HNE1.
We thank the reviewer to pointing this out – but we are indeed comparing the structure of CN and wt CN, both bound to NHE1. We agree completely that an ‘apple to orange’ comparison would need to be highlighted – but this is a true ‘apple to apple’ analysis.
17. In the final part of the “results” section, which concludes the findings, I am missing an important sentence, that is that E282K shifts the overall substrate preference of CN (the major conclusion of the study).
Per the reviewer we have added a sentence summarizing the major conclusion of the structure to the final part of the results section.
18. “Because PPPs are metalloenzymes, with the residues that coordinate the metal binding being 100% conserved between the family members, this enzyme family, unlike many kinase families, mostly lacks specificity at the active site.35,36” – many enzyme classes will have identical catalytic residues (ie. ion coordination in this particular case) while at the same time particular representatives of the class may largely differ in substrate preference because they differ in residues directly adjacent to catalytic residues which adjacent residues will modulate specificity. Please, rephrase this fragment – active site is broader term than the catalytic residues.
The reviewer is correct that the active site is broader than the core catalytic residues. For the PPP family, this is a key issue; indeed, PPP conservation extends much beyond the core catalytic residues explaining, in part, why no specific inhibitors for individual members of this family have been identified. Natural compounds bind with nearly identical K s to the family of enzymes. The only slight outlier is indeed CN; one reason for this is the identified i-1 binding pocket that we report here.
19. “This CN active site recruitment is sufficiently enhanced that it enabled the structure of CN bound to a PKA phosphorylated substrate to be determined.” – please rephrase. The substrate contained additional tether.
We are not certain how to rephrase the sentence, as the active site interaction is really driven by the active site i-1 binding event. We do want to highlight that we have tried to get substrate-bound structures of a PPP for many years (since 2010) and have continuously failed (so have indeed several groups). Even when substrates were tethered in a variety of ways (many unpublished experiments) there was never significant electron density identified around the active site, but rather only at some tethered sites (i.e. SLiM sites etc.). Thus, while the tether is overall important for binding (rationale for doing it), we can assure the reviewer that only additional binding at the active site – such as the i-1 site here at CN – allows for enough interaction strength to see electron density in the structures, i.e. to be able to trace a model of the structure.
20. “by creating a peptide library from PPP-inhibited HeLa cells and HEK293T cells expressing CNWT and CNE282K“ – please, be more exact. The peptide library in HeLa experiment was prepared at a very different stage of experiment and served a different purpose than in 239T so should not be combined in a single sentence.
Changed as requested:
Indeed, by creating a peptide library from PPP-inhibited HeLa cells and by testing sequence specificity in HEK293T and N2A cells expressing CNWT and CNE282K, we showed that an arginine residue at the i-1 site allows for enhanced CN active site recruitment.
21. “active site recruitment is necessary for a broad range of peptide sequences” – meaning unclear – please, rephrase.
Please see response to point 20. Thank you.
22. “…but, as we show, globally alters substrate preference from basophilic to acidophilic both in vitro and in cells.” – indicate that the cells used in the experiment are not relevant to physiological role of CN in the clinical pathology.
As requested, we defined the cell lines now in detail.
Thus, its mutation to a lysine reverses its charge from acidic to basic and weakens not only the recruitment and dephosphorylation of basophilic substrates like TAK1 but, as we show, globally alters substrate preference from basophilic to acidophilic both in vitro and in cells (here tested in HEK293T and N2A cell lines).
23. “These results not only provide a molecular basis for altered signaling in patients with the E282K variant” – tone down. The results do not provide any data on the influence of E282K on signaling in a setup relevant to pathology.
The sentence reads as follows:
These results not only provide a molecular basis for altered signaling in patients with the E282K variant but will enable future detailed CN proteomics studies to understand the consequences on specific CN substrates.
We agree with the reviewer that at this point we do not show data on the influence of CN on signaling in a setup relevant to pathology, but neither do we claim this here. Rather we only highlight that we have identified the molecular basis for the altered signaling that is performed by CN , which now can be leveraged in future studies to hopefully start to understand the specific changes in signaling, which is really highlighted already in the second part of the sentence.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have provided additional data which in my opinion strengthens the original conclusions. At the same time, the changes to the manuscript text do not entirely reflect the new insight gained with the additional data provided (especially regarding structural biology / biochemistry part). Also, some additional, minor experiments are still missing. I therefore suggest further modifications to the manuscript text and accepting the communication after those changes are introduces.
Major reservations
1. Comment: „How do affinities of fragments of TAK1…” – the reviewer appreciates the similar behavior of TAK1306-590 and TAK1384-474 in the performed assays. My original question however was if TAK11-606 behaves similarly to TAK1306-590 (and TAK1384-474), and this question has not been addressed. While using truncated variants of proteins in biophysical studies is a common practice and it is generally assumed that functional domains of a protein (in this case the kinase domain and IDR domain) act independently, this is rarely tested and not always true. One cannot exclude that the kinase domain of TAK1 influences the affinity of the C-terminal IDR.
The reviewer appreciates the difficulties in expressing and handling full length proteins, but at least a comment towards the untested possibility of kinase domain influencing the binding affinity of C-terminal IDR should be made in the manuscript. Also, the authors should avoid referring to TAK1384-474 as TAK1 which suggests a full length protein.
Even stronger reservation goes towards the rebuttal provided for RII. The fact that everybody uses the same truncated variant is not a proof that it fully reflects the physiological situation. Again, appreciating the experimental difficulties, a relevant comment should be made in the manuscript following the information provided in the rebuttal.
Frankly pointing out the limitations of the model allow the readers to take them into account while interpreting the data.
2. Comment: “The effect of mutating sites i-2 and i-3 in CN…”. Asp285 and Tyr315 are now arbitrarily removed from the description of CN binding pocket which is poorly justified since Asp285 seems to form the side of i-3 site while Tyr315 seems to form a stacking interaction with Arg(i-3) (though difficult to judge analyzing only 2D images). The description of the pocket at the end of part “The RRRS phosphosite motif binds CN near the active site” should be based on solid structural criteria and not tied to later findings pertaining to the importance of particular residues. These structural criteria are more than hydrogen bonds as multiple other interactions (including stacking and vdW constraints) are involved. In analyzing the pocket authors should use an unbiased methodology characteristic for structural biology and refrain from describing the pocket through the lens of further functional findings (ie. removing residues Asp285 and Tyr315 from the description, while the authors themselves considered those residues of importance in the prior version of the manuscript, to the extent they tested their effects in functional assays).
Further text in chapter “Arginine i-1 phosphosite recruitment is critical for efficient TAK1 dephosphorylation” refers to E282, Q284 and D285 and some “additional” residues, mysteriously selected in the absence of systematic description of the binding site in the proceeding chapter. Clearly defining the interactions at i-1, i-2 and i-3 sites in the prior chapter would justify the selection of residues for functional assays in the following chapter.
The activity and affinity data should be discussed together, instead of separately, to allow a holistic picture.
The new data provided in review consistently show the importance of i-1 site and more difficult to explain role of i-2 and i-3 sites. Mutations at i-1 site (E282K, E237K) decrease activity (Figure 2f) and affinity (Table S1; only shown for E282K; E237K should be included to complete the description of the i-1 site). Effects for sites i-2 and i-3 are also consistent. Q284K, D285K, Y315A increase activity (Figure 2f) while having little effect on affinity (Table S1; Y315A should be included to complete the description of the site).
Despite such consistent data, the description in the revised manuscript is inconsistent. Tyr315 has been omitted form the description of the binding pocket, while the residue is tested among the mutants evaluating the contribution of particular interactions in the pocket (Figure 2f). The description in the text focuses solely on i-1 effects while neglecting effects of equal strength, but opposite quality (increased vs. decreased activity) for sites i-2 and i-3. The text should consistently describe i-1 pocket (E282, E237), i-2 interaction (E284) and i-3 site (Y315, D285), and include the effects of mutations at site i-1 (decreased affinity and activity) and i-2 and i-3 (little effect on affinity and increased activity), even though the reason for the increased activity of mutants at i-2 and i-3 sites is not entirely clear (which should also be directly mentioned; Reviewer #3 also expressed this reservation about the same thing and yet it has not been addressed in the revised version neither as mine. The reason for the increased activity is simply unclear – it should be explicitly stated in the revised version).
Authors also mention testing Ri-3 and Ri-2 variants, but I can’t find the results demonstrating the effect of Ri-3 and Ri-2 on dephosphorylation rate by WT CN (only on E282K; Figure 4).
3. Comment: “E237K and E282K reduce activity of CN in dephosphorylating TAK1.”
Constructively addressed with data summarized at Figure 4g.
4. Comment: “The variant 436RRVS439…”
The variant has been tested with E282K, but I can’t find the results demonstrating the influence on dephosphorylation rate by WT CN.
5. Comment: “Chapter “Arginine in the i-1 position…”
I still fail to recognize that two examples justify calling a mechanism “general”, but the rest of the explanation clarifies my reservations.
6. Comment: “crystal structure of a substrate trapped CN complex”
Thank you for the clarification. It was clearly my omission. All the data were indeed present in the original manuscript.
7. Comment: “RII dephosphorylation…”
Constructively addressed.
8. Comment: “we determined the crystal structure of CNE282K“
Thank you for a clear clarification. In such a case, please modify the sentence “bound to NHE1, a substrate that binds CN using a PxIxIT and LxVP motif” by changing the world “substrate” into a “peptide”. A peptide lacking the dephosphorylation residues is not a substrate and the statement is misleading.
9. Comment “Is the (i-1) arginine containing structure exceptional…”
Constructively addressed.
10. Comment: “My major comment pertains to the phosphoproteome study…”
The authors have constructively addressed the reviewers reservation for the most part. It is useful to see that experiments in less mechanistic and more physiological setting are ongoing, but due to their length, complexity and scope beyond the mechanistic interest of this manuscript delaying its publication while waiting for their completion would not have been justified.
However, I still ask to address the following point:
a. It should be clearly stated that because Lys-C is used for digestion all the potential sites having K(i-1) are not detected – unless relevant provisions were made in data analysis which should also be mentioned.
11. Comment: “As it is now,…”
Constructively addressed
Minor comments
1. Please, rephrase: “Mutating either of these SLiMs abolishes their ability to be dephosphorylated by CN, …”. It is not SLiMs that get dephosphorylated.
2. “Recent work has also shown that the efficacy of CN catalysis can be modulated by…” – remove “also”
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: It is well apparent that the authors have considered the concerns of the reviewers and have done a thorough effort to either address these concerns through new experimentation, edits to the manuscript text or have provided acceptable rationale in their response to the reviewers explaining the limits to the scope of the current study. The revisions have strengthened the manuscript and I have no major remaining concerns. I recommend acceptance.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The comments have been addressed appropriately, including the addition of new experiments (ITC to determine Kd) and improvements to the representation of structures in some of the figures.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our work. It is great to read that our additional data strengthens the original conclusions.
Major reservations
1. Comment: „How do affinities of fragments of TAK1…” – the reviewer appreciates the similar behavior of TAK1306-590 and TAK1384-474 in the performed assays. My original question however was if TAK11-606 behaves similarly to TAK1306-590 (and TAK1384-474), and this question has not been addressed. While using truncated variants of proteins in biophysical studies is a common practice and it is generally assumed that functional domains of a protein (in this case the kinase domain and IDR domain) act independently, this is rarely tested and not always true. One cannot exclude that the kinase domain of TAK1 influences the affinity of the C-terminal IDR.
The reviewer is correct that the potential influence(s) of intradomain interactions on specific biochemical assays are not commonly tested, especially in the absence of published cellular data that would indicate that such interactions might have functional importance. We have tested for such interdomain interactions in other biological systems, such as those highlighted here. Our data have not detected effects in the cases tested. Rather, our work and that of others have shown that long IDRs like that present in TAK1 almost exclusively function independently from the folded domains present within the same protein. This is indeed not a surprise. While the kinase domain (residues ~26-300) has dimensions of ~35x35x50 Å, the dimensions of the IDR tested here (residues 306-590) can reach a length of ~850 Å when fully extended; thus, at any point in time, the vast majority of the IDR residues are very far from the kinase domain. For these reasons, it is highly unlikely that the kinase domain influences the affinity of the C-terminal IDR.
Finally, it is important to emphasize that, by definition, SLiMs are only identified in IDRs; thus, there is a clear physiological reason to focus on the IDR of TAK1 for mediating CN binding. Indeed, and as the reviewer knows, TAK1 activation requires that TAK1 binds another protein, namely TAB1 (TAB1 binds TAK1 via a structured helical interaction to the TAK1 kinase C-lobe). Here, we solely focus on the key interaction of TAK1 with CN. Clearly, it might be of interest for others to further investigate if CN also interacts with TAB1/2/3 as well (that said, thus far no SLiMs have been identified in TAB1). Furthermore, we have not seen TABs in our MS data and thus we have not followed up. We hope that this further strengthens the rationale why we chose to focus on the TAK1 IDR region in this manuscript.
The reviewer appreciates the difficulties in expressing and handling full length proteins, but at least a comment towards the untested possibility of kinase domain influencing the binding affinity of C-terminal IDR should be made in the manuscript. Also, the authors should avoid referring to TAK1384-474 as TAK1 which suggests a full length protein.
Even stronger reservation goes towards the rebuttal provided for RII. The fact that everybody uses the same truncated variant is not a proof that it fully reflects the physiological situation. Again, appreciating the experimental difficulties, a relevant comment should be made in the manuscript following the information provided in the rebuttal.
Frankly pointing out the limitations of the model allow the readers to take them into account while interpreting the data.
As requested, we added a statement that we did not test for the influence of other domains on the TAK1 IDR domain.
First, we modified the sentence:
Therefore, we tested if the TAK1 IDR binds CN using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC).
IDR was added to highlight that we only tested binding of CN to the IDR.
Second, we added the following sentence:
We did not test if CN binds to the TAK1 catalytic domain (likely not as no CN SLiM was identified) nor if the TAK1 catalytic domain makes an intramolecular interaction with the TAK1 C-terminal IDR.
We would like to keep the nomenclature as is – simply because the manuscript would gain significant length with the additional annotations, making it much harder to read. We are confident that the readers of Nature Communications will be able to distinguish the different domains as is – especially as they are detailed in the methods as well as clearly illustrated in the figures (including Figure 1).
2. Comment: “The effect of mutating sites i-2 and i-3 in CN…”. Asp285 and Tyr315 are now arbitrarily removed from the description of CN binding pocket which is poorly justified since Asp285 seems to form the side of i-3 site while Tyr315 seems to form a stacking interaction with Arg(i-3) (though difficult to judge analyzing only 2D images).
While we appreciate the careful review of reviewer 1, we disagree that anything we do or represent in the data has been done ‘arbitrarily’. As explained in our original rebuttal letter, we ‘updated Figure 2 to only highlight polar/ionic interactions that are <4 Å (i.e. to focus on only the most significant interactions); we also added the distances to the figure to further improve clarity.’ Clearly, using a number cutoff is not arbitrary but rather 100% reproducible.
We have requested all PDB files to be released (they will be released on 12/17/2025) – so the reviewer can see them in 3D. We are always happy to provide all data to the reviewer.
The description of the pocket at the end of part “The RRRS phosphosite motif binds CN near the active site” should be based on solid structural criteria and not tied to later findings pertaining to the importance of particular residues. These structural criteria are more than hydrogen bonds as multiple other interactions (including stacking and vdW constraints) are involved. In analyzing the pocket authors should use an unbiased methodology characteristic for structural biology and refrain from describing the pocket through the lens of further functional findings (ie. removing residues Asp285 and Tyr315 from the description, while the authors themselves considered those residues of importance in the prior version of the manuscript, to the extent they tested their effects in functional assays).
As highlighted above, and in response to the previous review, our revision implemented a rigorous and reproducible criteria for defining interactions: using distances for the structural analysis. As stated before, the original Figure 2 was suboptimal as it did not highlight widely differing distances. Indeed, the response highlights this issue. The distances highlighted in the original figure for Asp285 and Tyr315 are ≥ 5 Å (some even 6-7 Å) and thus have significantly less or no impact on binding (it was my oversight that these were included in the original submission). Indeed, we have now proven their lack of importance for TAK1 binding with the additional ITC experiments performed in the revised manuscript. Taken together the combined data ensures correct, rigorous and unbiased interpretation of the structural and functional data.
As stated, the original figure was poorly prepared in the sense that the differences in the distances, which typically correlate with interaction strength, were not illustrated, giving the incorrect impression that all interactions were equally important. I apologize for this oversight during the original submission – my mistake. In its current form, this paper includes 3 crystal structures, multiple NMR data sets, ITC experiments, biochemical and cellular studies, including multiple MS experiments carried out in 2 different cell lines. We always aim to describe our data to the highest standards and accuracy, and I did not achieve the highest level of quality on the original figure 2 – not because we did not aim for it – but rather because it simply ‘slipped through the cracks’. But the careful review ensured that this ‘crack’ is successfully closed – thank you for your careful review and help.
We have always followed (and will always follow) all structural biology standards (see Supplementary Table 2 and PDB file) for our data. However, the reviewer might also have not fully appreciated that we described in the manuscript (and highlighted in Supplemental Figure 3) that the interaction at the active site is dynamic (fuzzy) and indeed adopts at least 2 conformations that we captured in our structure. Thus, additional experiments will always be necessary to fully understand the complete picture of such a fuzzy interaction – this is what we have done here.
We have recently summarized some of the aspects of fuzzy interactions in catalysis in a review article – PMID: 40580813. We are sure many more of these interactions are identified that are not locked down into a single conformation and will require complementary techniques for their full descriptions.
Further text in chapter “Arginine i-1 phosphosite recruitment is critical for efficient TAK1 dephosphorylation” refers to E282, Q284 and D285 and some “additional” residues, mysteriously selected in the absence of systematic description of the binding site in the proceeding chapter. Clearly defining the interactions at i-1, i-2 and i-3 sites in the prior chapter would justify the selection of residues for functional assays in the following chapter.
We deleted the word ‘additional’.
The activity and affinity data should be discussed together, instead of separately, to allow a holistic picture.
The new data provided in review consistently show the importance of i-1 site and more difficult to explain role of i-2 and i-3 sites. Mutations at i-1 site (E282K, E237K) decrease activity (Figure 2f) and affinity (Table S1; only shown for E282K; E237K should be included to complete the description of the i-1 site). Effects for sites i-2 and i-3 are also consistent. Q284K, D285K, Y315A increase activity (Figure 2f) while having little effect on affinity (Table S1; Y315A should be included to complete the description of the site).
Despite such consistent data, the description in the revised manuscript is inconsistent.
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the excellent consistency of our data from different sources (X-ray, NMR, ITC, activity assays). This orthogonal approach is critical for describing complex data as presented in our work. We are certain that the current presentation allows for the best presentation of the complex data for a broad audience of Nature Communications and thank Reviewer 2 and 3, who clearly support the current presentation.
Tyr315 has been omitted form the description of the binding pocket, while the residue is tested among the mutants evaluating the contribution of particular interactions in the pocket (Figure 2f). The description in the text focuses solely on i-1 effects while neglecting effects of equal strength, but opposite quality (increased vs. decreased activity) for sites i-2 and i-3. The text should consistently describe i-1 pocket (E282, E237), i-2 interaction (E284) and i-3 site (Y315, D285), and include the effects of mutations at site i-1 (decreased affinity and activity) and i-2 and i-3 (little effect on affinity and increased activity), even though the reason for the increased activity of mutants at i-2 and i-3 sites is not entirely clear (which should also be directly mentioned; Reviewer #3 also expressed this reservation about the same thing and yet it has not been addressed in the revised version neither as mine. The reason for the increased activity is simply unclear – it should be explicitly stated in the revised version).
We want to highlight one more time that no data has been omitted from the manuscript, rather we display the data in the most coherent and clear way possible for the readers. Indeed, we are focusing on all the residues that have interactions that are 4 Å or less, as these are the most critical interactions (it is well established that ionic, polar and van der Waals interactions correlate with distance). We prove that this assumption is correct using ITC – where the data shows that only residues within the i-1 pocket have significant impacts on binding affinity with TAK1.
The reviewer is correct – we do not know the effect of increased activity for CN Y315A. We could speculate that it is most likely the change from a bulky tyrosine sidechain to a small alanine sidechain is the main driver, which allows, due to the reduced size, additional degrees of freedom of the substrate to dock for dephosphorylation, likely leading to increased dephosphorylation. We prefer not to speculate.
In the current manuscript, we solely focus on the i-1 interaction pocket, as it is completely novel.
Authors also mention testing Ri-3 and Ri-2 variants, but I can’t find the results demonstrating the effect of Ri-3 and Ri-2 on dephosphorylation rate by WT CN (only on E282K; Figure 4).
The reviewer is correct – we describe the data for CN E282K but compare it to the WT CN dephosphorylation in Figure 4. This is the only possible way to accurately describe the data as the ensemble of substrate structures (TAK1 ensemble) that is presented for CN dephosphorylation will change in each substrate variant, i.e. deletion of N-terminal arginine residues will change the interaction with the phosphorylated pS residue and thus change the ensemble of structure in the IDP for binding and subsequent dephosphorylation presentation. This does not happen for a small molecule substrate (DiFMUP or pNPP) or folded proteins, where such comparisons are possible. It is for this reason we did all experiments in a manner that changed CN and kept the substrate constant as otherwise we would have introduced a broad range of unknown factors, which would not lead to a rigorous comparison of the data.
3. Comment: “E237K and E282K reduce activity of CN in dephosphorylating TAK1.”
Constructively addressed with data summarized at Figure 4g.
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our data and work.
4. Comment: “The variant 436RRVS439…”
The variant has been tested with E282K, but I can’t find the results demonstrating the influence on dephosphorylation rate by WT CN.
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our data and work. We want to refer to our detailed response above.
5. Comment: “Chapter “Arginine in the i-1 position…”
I still fail to recognize that two examples justify calling a mechanism “general”, but the rest of the explanation clarifies my reservations.
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our data and work.
6. Comment: “crystal structure of a substrate trapped CN complex”
Thank you for the clarification. It was clearly my omission. All the data were indeed present in the original manuscript.
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our data and work.
7. Comment: “RII dephosphorylation…”
Constructively addressed.
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our data and work.
8. Comment: “we determined the crystal structure of CNE282K“
Thank you for a clear clarification. In such a case, please modify the sentence “bound to NHE1, a substrate that binds CN using a PxIxIT and LxVP motif” by changing the world “substrate” into a “peptide”. A peptide lacking the dephosphorylation residues is not a substrate and the statement is misleading.
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our data and work. We are not fully convinced that using the word peptide make this easier to understand (especially, as a peptide has no meaning regarding a biological function of a protein, and NHE1 is not a random peptide that we created by design, but rather it has a specific function and way to interact with CN, which has been investigated in high detail in a previous manuscript that is cited in our work).
Nevertheless, as requested we changed the word to peptide.
9. Comment “Is the (i-1) arginine containing structure exceptional…”
Constructively addressed.
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our data and work.
10. Comment: “My major comment pertains to the phosphoproteome study…”
The authors have constructively addressed the reviewers reservation for the most part. It is useful to see that experiments in less mechanistic and more physiological setting are ongoing, but due to their length, complexity and scope beyond the mechanistic interest of this manuscript delaying its publication while waiting for their completion would not have been justified.
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our data and work.
However, I still ask to address the following point:
a. It should be clearly stated that because Lys-C is used for digestion all the potential sites having K(i-1) are not detected – unless relevant provisions were made in data analysis which should also be mentioned.
If the reviewer is referring to the dephosphorylation assays in original submitted Figure 5D then the reviewer is correct, the K in the i-1 position might be lost due to the Lys-C digest. However, because of the reviewers’ concerns in the last round of reviews, we already deleted this figure in the originally revised manuscript (R1).
If the reviewer refers to the in-cell data shown in Figures 5 and 6 (as well as Supplemental Figure 8), the dephosphorylation occurs before digest. So, in these data we can clearly assay K in the i-1 position. We hope this clarifies the concerns of the reviewer.
11. Comment: “As it is now,…”
Constructively addressed
We thank the reviewer for her/his support of our data and work.
Minor comments
1. Please, rephrase: “Mutating either of these SLiMs abolishes their ability to be dephosphorylated by CN, …”. It is not SLiMs that get dephosphorylated.
Thank you – done.
rephrased to:
Mutating either of these SLiMs in substrates abolishes dephosphorylation by CN,
2. “Recent work has also shown that the efficacy of CN catalysis can be modulated by…” – remove “also”
Thank you – done.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
We thank reviewer 2 for her/his support of our work.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
We thank reviewer 3 for her/his support of our work.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have made substantial improvements to the presented data in round R1 of the review and clarified the remaining issues in their detailed rebuttal letter in round R2. With the additional data and explanations provided I find the current manuscript an excellently presented and very interesting piece of data. I recommend publication of the manuscript in its current form.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Recently, de novo heterozygous variants of Calcineurin (CN) were reported as the cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder that presents with epileptic encephalopathy and dysmorphism (DEE91), with the largest group of patients harboring the CN missense mutation E282K (glutamate → lysine). Here, we use molecular and cellular techniques to define how this mutation alters CN activity. We discover that basophilic substrates use an arginine residue to bind to CN via an acidic substrate recruitment pocket adjacent to the CN active site, the E282 pocket. Furthermore, we show that basic residues in the i-1 position of the substrate relative to the substrate phosphosite enhance CN-mediated dephosphorylation. While the CN E282K structure shows that the overall conformation is unchanged, the E282 pocket transforms from acidic to basic, with pocket access blocked by the formation of a E282K-E237 salt bridge. Finally, in vitro assays and in cell phosphoproteomics show that CN E282K shifts CN substrate dephosphorylation profiles from basic to acidic, thereby altering CN-mediated dephosphorylation signaling. Together, these data define the molecular impact of the CN E282K variant in cells and development, providing a key step for developing strategies to treat this disorder and its accompanying complications.

---

## Introduction

Phosphorylation is one of the most ubiquitous, reversible post-translational modifications (PTM) in cells1. Thus, defining the finely tuned specific and reciprocal relationship between kinases and phosphatases is essential for understanding their control and modulation of signaling pathways. Calcineurin (CN, Protein Phosphatase 2B [PP2B], PP3)2–4 is a ubiquitously expressed phosphoprotein phosphatase (PPP) that is especially abundant in the brain. Upon activation by Ca2+ (hence calcineurin)5, CN dephosphorylates an estimated 100–1000s of substrates to regulate development, synaptic plasticity, learning and memory as well as many other functions3,6,7. As a consequence, disruption of CN-regulated signaling in the brain has, for decades, been associated with disease, including Alzheimer’s (AD)8 and Parkinson’s disease9. Large-scale whole exome sequencing (WES) has greatly advanced the identification of genetic variants that underlie disease, especially rare diseases. During the last decade, WES studies have identified multiple de novo variants of CN (PPP3CA) that are associated with a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder that presents with epileptic encephalopathy, intellectual disabilities, dysmorphism, hypotonia and autism spectrum disorder (PPP3CA-related DEE91 [developmental and epileptic encephalopathy]; OMIM #617711)10–14, with the missense mutation E282K being the most frequently observed variant. Critically, the molecular mechanisms by which these de novo CN variants, including E282K, disrupt CN-mediated signaling are major open questions.

CN is a constitutive heterodimer with two subunits (Fig. 1a)5,15. The catalytic subunit A (CNA) contains the active site, the calmodulin binding region and an auto-inhibitory domain (AID). The regulatory subunit B (CNB) binds four Ca2+ ions, making CN responsive to calcium signaling. Substrates and regulators are recruited to CN via CN-specific short linear motifs (SLiMs), short conserved sequences that are present within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins that mediate protein:protein interactions16–24. The PxIxIT SLiM binds the CNA subunit16,20,21,23,24 while the LxVP SLiM binds the interface between the CNA and Ca2+-sensing CNB domain21; the latter is accessible only upon Ca2+-activation18,25,26. CN substrates, such as the NFATs17,18,22, NHE120,27, RCAN123, among others, use both PxIxIT and LxVP motifs to bind CN in a 1-to-1 manner. Mutating these SLiMs in substrates abolishes dephosphorylation by CN, demonstrating the essential role of recruitment for substrate dephosphorylation18–21. As a consequence, simply blocking substrate recruitment is sufficient to inhibit CN-mediated dephosphorylation in cells, a mechanism exploited by viruses (i.e., A238L of the African swine fever virus) and immunosuppressants such as FK50621,28,29.

Recent work has shown that the efficacy of CN catalysis can be modulated by additional mechanisms. For example, a recently discovered CN active site recognition sequence (TxxP) enhances recruitment to the active site, accelerating CN-mediated dephosphorylation20. However, many CN substrates do not have a phosphosite TxxP sequence, suggesting there may be additional mechanisms for enhancing phosphosite dephosphorylation. One such possibility is the enhanced binding of kinase-specific phosphosite sequences that are targeted by CN for dephosphorylation. For example, CN counteracts the activities of basophilic kinases, especially PKA, which requires an R-R-x-S/T motif for productive phosphorylation30. How and if this basophilic kinase motif is locally recruited to the CN active site for dephosphorylation processing remains an open question.

By leveraging two model PKA/CN substrate pairs, here we show an additional recruitment pocket adjacent to the CN active site that is critical for CN substrate recruitment, specificity and regulation. The two substrates include the canonical PKA regulatory subunit II (RII)31 that via a phosphorylation switch, controls PKA activity proceeding cAMP-binding, and the transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) activated kinase (MAP Kinase Kinase Kinase 7 or Transforming growth factor β-activated kinase 1; TAK1)32. Leveraging both an in vitro peptide and cell-based proteomics approach, we tested how this pocket globally affects local CN active site recruitment. Our comprehensive structural, biochemical and proteomics data reveals that an arginine residue at the i-1 position relative to the phosphosite in CN substrates is critical for enhanced recruitment and dephosphorylation of these substrates. This enabled us to define an additional CN substrate recruitment pocket that facilitates recruitment of basophilic substrates. Furthermore, we show that this CN substrate recruitment pocket includes the major clinical CN variant residue E282, highlighting that the E282K variant likely results in a global shift of signaling outcomes resulting in neurodevelopment deficits. Defining how CN recruits and especially dephosphorylates distinct CN-specific substrates will not only advance our understanding of the role of PPPs in modulating signaling pathways, but also provide the data needed to understand how the de novo CN variants alter this signaling and, in turn, lead to the development of routes for treating PPP3CA-related DEE91.

---

## Results

TAK1 uses an LxVP SLiM and a RRRS motif to bind CN
TAK1 is a mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) that contains an N-terminal kinase domain (Fig. 1a; aa 1–306) and a C-terminal IDR (Fig. 1a; aa 306–606) that is phosphorylated by PKA at Ser439 (436RRRS439). CN counteracts the activities of many basophilic kinases, including PKA, and its sequence contains a putative LxVP motif (422LDVP425) near the PKA phosphorylation site22. Therefore we tested if the TAK1 IDR binds CN using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). The data showed that both the extended C-terminal IDR (TAK1 306–590) and a shorter version including the target phosphorylation site (TAK1 384–474; hereafter, TAK1) bind CN and do so with nearly identical affinities (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Fig. 1a, b; Supplementary Table 1). Consistent with these data the 2D [1H,15N] heteronuclear single quantum coherence (HSQC) spectra of TAK1 306–590 and TAK1 show an early perfect overlap of all HN/N cross-peaks, confirming there were no local or long-range changes between the ensemble of conformations adopted in both TAK1 constructs (Supplementary Fig. 1c). We did not test if CN binds to the TAK1 catalytic domain (likely not as no CN SLiM was identified) nor if the TAK1 catalytic domain makes an intramolecular interaction with the TAK1 C-terminal IDR.

To identify the TAK1 residues that bind CN, we completed the sequence-specific backbone assignment of TAK1 (Supplementary Fig. 2a) and overlaid the 2D [1H,15N] HSQC spectra of 15N-labeled TAK1 in the absence and presence of CN (Fig. 1c, d). Many HN/N cross-peaks were significantly broadened with CN (Fig. 1d, e; Supplementary Fig. 2b–e), with most reduced intensities corresponding to TAK1 residues 415–441 (Fig. 1e; includes the putative LxVP motif and residues surrounding the Ser439 PKA phosphosite). We confirmed the importance of the LxVP motif for CN recruitment using ITC, as a variant lacking the LxVP sequence (LxVP dead: 422LDVP425 → 422AAAA425) failed to bind CN (Fig. 1f). TAK1 bound CN with an atypically strong affinity compared to other LxVP:CN interactions (TAK1 KD, 823 ± 8 nM; Fig. 1b; other reported LxVP KD’s, ~1800–500,000 nM; Supplementary Table 1)21,23,33, suggesting that residues outside the LxVP motif contribute to CN binding. Consistent with this, in the presence of CN, the peak intensities of the consensus site for PKA phosphorylation (436RRRS439) were reduced to the same extent as those observed for the LxVP residues (Fig. 1e). To test if these residues facilitate CN binding, we mutated the PKA phosphorylation consensus sequence in TAK1 (RRR dead: 436RRRS439 → 436AAAS439; Fig. 1a) and measured its affinity for CN. The affinity decreased ~4.5-fold (Fig. 1g, Supplementary Table 1), demonstrating that 436RRR438 enhances CN binding. Together, these data show that TAK1 strictly requires a functional LxVP motif to bind CN and that this is strengthened by the RRRS phosphosite motif.

The RRRS phosphosite motif binds CN near the active site
To define how the RRRS motif binds CN, we determined the crystal structure of a substrate-trapped CN complex. Trapping was achieved by using a catalytically inactive CN variant (D90A; lacks the M1 active site metal and thus is unable to dephosphorylate substrates) and a thiophosphorylated TAK1 substrate (tp, thiophosphorylated; hereafter, CN D90A:tpTAK1, Fig. 2a, b; tethered to the PxIxIT site using CN-specific the A238L viral inhibitor peptide, Supplementary Fig. 3a, b, Supplementary Table 2). Two copies of the CN D90A:tpTAK1 complex were present in the asymmetric unit, with clear electron density for TAK1 residues bound to the CN LxVP binding pocket and the CN active site (Fig. 2b–d; Supplementary Fig. 3c–g; aa 422–428, 435–442; no density was observed for aa 429–434, which form a dynamic linker between the LxVP binding pocket and CN active site). The TAK1 LxVP motif (422LDVP425) binds the CN LxVP binding pocket in a manner identical to those observed previously (Fig. 2c). TAK1 Leu422 and Val424 bind two deep hydrophobic pockets at the CNA/B interface. Electron density was also observed at the CN active site, corresponding to TAK1 residues 436RRRtpS439 (Fig. 2c, d). While the conformations of the Leu422 and Val424 side chains were nearly identical between the two copies of TAK1 in the asymmetric unit, as is typical for buried hydrophobic interactions, the arginine side chains of the RRRS motif (436RRR438) adopted slightly different conformations between the two copies, highlighting that these charge:charge interactions are more dynamic (i.e., fuzzy; Supplementary Figs. 3c–g). TAK1 arginine residues bind an extended acidic pocket on CN (Fig. 2d), making polar and/or ionic interactions (<4 Å) with CN residues Glu282 and Gln284 (100% conserved in CN from yeast to humans; Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. 3h). Arg438 (R i-1 relative to tpS), which is immediately adjacent to the active site, makes the most extensive interactions with CN, binding a deep, strongly acidic pocket defined by Glu237 and Glu282 (Fig. 2e).

Arginine i-1 phosphosite recruitment facilitates efficient TAK1 dephosphorylation
To quantify the contribution of these CN residues for TAK1 binding, we performed ITC measurements of TAK1 vs CN WT, CN E282K, CN Q284K and CN D285K. The data showed that affinity of TAK1 for CN E282K is 3-fold weaker than CN WT (akin to TAK1 RRR dead; Supplementary Fig. 4a, Supplementary Table 1), while binding is only minimally impacted for TAK1 vs CN Q284K or CN D285K (Supplementary Fig. 4b, c Supplementary Table 1). These data highlight the key role of the R i-1 residue for binding. Next, we performed CN dephosphorylation assays. We mutated these residues in the CN substrate binding pocket and measured their ability to dephosphorylate TAK1 pSer439 (uniformly PKA-phosphorylated Ser439, pS439, was achieved using the TAK1 S389A/S417A variant, as NMR experiments showed that in vitro Ser389 and Ser417 are partially, non-specifically phosphorylated by PKA). The data showed that CN variants with mutations in residues near the i-2 and i-3 arginine residues (Q284K, D285K, Y315A), had an increase in activity (Fig. 2f). In contrast, mutating the residues that define the CN i-1 pocket—E237K and E282K—significantly reduced activity, by ~50% and ~70%, respectively (Fig. 2f, Table 1). To further confirm that the arginine in the i-1 position facilitates TAK1 binding at the active site, we generated the TAK1 R438V variant (436RRRS439 → 436RRVS439) and measured its affinity for CN and CN E282K using ITC (Supplementary Fig. 4d, Supplementary Table 1). The data showed that the lack of an arginine in the i-1 position weakens the affinity ~3-fold, nearly to the same extent observed for the TAK1 RRR dead variant, but, as reasoned, has very minimal effect on CN binding (Supplementary Fig. 4e, Supplementary Table 1). Together, these data identify a negatively charged pocket, the E282 pocket, that facilitates the recruitment and dephosphorylation of substrates containing an arginine residue in the i-1 position (R i-1).

Arginine in the i-1 position is a general mechanism for enhanced CN substrate dephosphorylation
We next tested the generality of an arginine in the i-1 position for enhancing CN-mediated recruitment and dephosphorylation of CN substrates by measuring the dephosphorylation of a canonical CN substrate that lacks an i-1 arginine: the PKA regulatory subunit RII (RII Ser99 is phosphorylated and dephosphorylated by PKA and CN, respectively, and lacks an i-1 arginine, 96RRVS99; RII 44–103 construct used for these studies; hereafter RII). We also created an RII variant where the i-1 residue was mutated to arginine (Fig. 3a; i-1.e., contains an R i-1). Like TAK1, RII also uses an LxVP motif for CN recruitment, which we confirmed using NMR spectroscopy and X-ray crystallography (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 5a–d, Supplementary Table 2). To assay CN-mediated dephosphorylation, we phosphorylated Ser99 in wt RII and the RII V98R variant (RII V98R; 96RRVS99 → 96RRRS99) using PKA (phosphorylation assays performed using the RII S58A/S78A construct to ensure phosphorylation of only Ser99). The data showed that replacing Val98 with an arginine in the RII i-1 position enhanced CN-mediated dephosphorylation by ~50% compared to WT, confirming the enhanced dephosphorylation of substrates with an arginine in the i-1 position (Fig. 3b; Table 2). Second, while the i-1 pocket charge reversal variants CN E237K and CN E282K reduced the dephosphorylation of wt RII, the decrease in activity was significantly more pronounced with the RII V98R variant, by ~70% and ~85%, respectively (Fig. 3b; Table 2). Together, these data confirm the role of the acidic binding pocket adjacent to the CN active site, the E282 binding pocket, for CN substrate recruitment of R i-1 containing substrates.

CN E282K fails to effectively recruit R i-1-dependent CN substrates
These results show that the CN E282 binding pocket has a critical role in recruiting R i-1-containing substrates to the CN active site to facilitate their dephosphorylation. The most frequently observed variant in PPP3CA-related DEE91 is E282K (Fig. 4a).
